title: LLMs Get Lost When Intent Keeps Moving
hook: Real users don't state what they want up front — they reveal, revise, and redirect it mid-conversation. Rewrite existing benchmarks that way and scores drop across every model family.
key_points: A framework converts static single-turn tasks into multi-turn conversations where the user's intent evolves across turns.
Intent is incrementally revealed, revised, and sometimes redirected mid-conversation, while each task's original evaluation protocol is preserved.
Because the protocol is untouched, existing benchmarks become controlled testbeds with no new annotation.
Strong static-setting performance does not transfer: the authors report substantial drops across multiple model families.
The failure is invisible to standard single-turn evaluation, yet central to any model deployed as a collaborator.
content_html: As LLMs get deployed as collaborators rather than one-shot answerers, they take on tasks through back-and-forth. But genuine interaction is dynamic: users rarely lay out what they want at the start. They disclose it piecemeal, revise it once they see a draft, and sometimes change direction entirely. Training and evaluation, meanwhile, are still overwhelmingly single-turn and fully specified.
extra_html:
Reusing benchmarks instead of building one

Rather than writing a new dataset, the authors build a framework that transforms static single-turn tasks into multi-turn conversations where the user's intent evolves — incrementally revealed, revised, and at times redirected mid-conversation. Crucially, each task's original evaluation protocol is preserved, so existing benchmarks become controlled testbeds for the dynamic setting without any new annotation. That makes the comparison clean: same task, same scoring, only the delivery of intent changes.

The result

Across multiple tasks the pattern is consistent — strong static-setting performance does not transfer, with substantial drops across model families. The authors' reading is that today's LLMs don't yet faithfully track and act on a user's evolving intent, and that this is exactly the kind of capability static evaluation cannot see while being central to anything you'd call a collaborative agent. Tack, Laban, and Neville, arXiv 2026.

related.title: AI Tutors Jump In Too Soon
related.hook: Put an LLM in the tutor's seat and it interrupts sooner and more often than a human would — and hands over the whole solution where a person would have offered a hint.

related.title: Attractor States Emerge in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations
related.hook: Let two LLMs debate long enough and one model's style pulls the other toward it — Claude Haiku drags partners into its own habits, while GPT-4.1 nano is easily swayed.

related.title: Plans Don't Persist: Context Management Is Load-Bearing for Agents
related.hook: An agent writes a plan, then context compression evicts it. This paper shows the plan never became internal state — once it leaves the window, the agent forgets it and task success craters.

flashcards.prompt: What does the paper's framework change about an existing benchmark, and what does it deliberately leave alone?
flashcards.back_html: It turns each single-turn task into a multi-turn conversation with evolving user intent, while preserving the task's original evaluation protocol — so no new annotation is needed.

flashcards.prompt: What is the paper's central finding about evolving-intent conversations?

choices.text: Strong static-setting performance does not transfer — models drop substantially once intent is revealed and revised over turns
Models handle evolving intent well, but only when the user is explicit about changing their mind
Larger models close the gap entirely, so it is purely a scale problem

flashcards.explanation_html: The drop shows up across model families, which is why the authors frame it as a capability gap rather than a quirk of one model or size.

flashcards.prompt: Why is this gap described as invisible to standard evaluation?
flashcards.back_html: Benchmarks predominantly present tasks as single-turn and fully specified, so a model that cannot track intent as it shifts still scores well.
